syllabus.clause: write path: durable log append → memtable → rotate to an immutable memtable → flush as a sorted SSTable. Reads check the newest structures first. Immutable flushed files simplify concurrent reads and recovery.

items.item: The overwrite claim deliberately flushes the SSTable before the overwrite happens, so the stale value genuinely exists on disk at the moment of the overwrite; a fresh get() against the same key afterward can only return the new value by actually checking the active memtable first, not by the SSTable never having held a conflicting value in the first place.

at.step: Measured: the fresh overwrite genuinely won over the stale, flushed value

items.item: The fall-through claim measures a real checked-structure count returned by the lookup itself, not an assumption about which structure should have been checked, so the oldest key's higher cost and the newest key's lower cost are both genuine consequences of the real read path's own newest-first order.

at.step: Measured: the oldest key genuinely took checking more than one structure, the newest key took checking only the active memtable, and a lookup for a key that doesn't exist at all had to check every single structure that exists

items.item: The immutability claim uses a content fold over the SSTable's own entry bytes taken immediately after flush and again after several further reads (hits and misses both), rather than merely asserting no mutating method exists on the type, so the claim is a genuine before-and-after measurement, not a structural guarantee taken on faith.

at.step: Measured: a flushed SSTable's own bytes genuinely never changed across many later reads against it, hits and misses alike

items.item: This topic's own memtable, immutable-memtable list, and SSTable list are all plain in-memory Rust collections rather than real files, continuing this chapter's own stated convention that nothing here needs real file I/O, root access, or special hardware; the write-ahead log itself is represented only as a generation counter, since the claims under test are about read-path ordering and SSTable immutability, not log durability.

at.step: A key's value gets written, then its memtable is flushed to an SSTable. The same key is then overwritten, but that new write never gets flushed. Which value does a read actually return: the old, flushed one, or the new, unflushed one?

items.item: The three-key fall-through scenario deliberately rotates and flushes twice before the final key is written, so the oldest key ends up in the very first SSTable created rather than merely in some SSTable, making the newest-to-oldest check order the genuine reason that key costs more to find.

at.step: Measured: the oldest key genuinely took checking more than one structure, the newest key took checking only the active memtable, and a lookup for a key that doesn't exist at all had to check every single structure that exists
